scene.testo: Every single day, an invisible storm of radiation passes straight through your body in orbit, and it is about 200 times stronger than what you get on the ground. Yet astronauts on the space station walk home alive, healthy, and ready to fly again.

So what is really happening out there? Why doesn't radiation kill astronauts on the space station? Imagine particles moving near the speed of light, slicing through the walls, through your skin, through your bones, and you feel absolutely nothing.

But the real danger is not what hits you today. It is what quietly adds up over months. Tonight, the truth about radiation in space, and the invisible shield that keeps the crew alive. Stay with me, because the biggest surprise comes at the very end.

Imagine you are floating inside the International Space Station at 6 AM. The air hums softly. Fans whisper. Your sleeping bag is clipped to the wall, and your arms drift up in front of you like you are underwater.

The station circles Earth about 250 miles up, roughly the distance from New York City to Washington D.C., straight overhead. It travels at 17,500 miles per hour, and completes one full lap around the planet about every 90 minutes.

That means 16 sunrises and 16 sunsets every single day. Your 6 AM is just a number on a clock. The crew follows Greenwich Mean Time, and the lights inside are dimmed and brightened to fake a normal day.

You unzip the bag, push off the wall, and glide toward the galley. Everything feels safe. Soft light, warm air, a laptop with today's checklist. But just inches beyond that wall, space is anything but gentle.

Outside, the temperature swings from about 250 degrees Fahrenheit in sunlight to around minus 250 degrees Fahrenheit in shadow. There is no air. And there is something else out there that you can never see, hear, or smell. Radiation.

Radiation is energy traveling as waves or as fast moving particles. Some of it can knock electrons off atoms, even inside your cells. That is called ionizing radiation, and it can damage DNA, the instruction manual inside every cell of your body.

Where does it come from? Three main sources. First, the Sun, which constantly blows a stream of charged particles called the solar wind. Second, giant solar eruptions. And third, galactic cosmic rays, particles from exploded stars far beyond our solar system.

Galactic cosmic rays are the nastiest. Some are heavy atomic nuclei moving at a large fraction of the speed of light. They are rare, but a single one can punch through metal, through plastic, and through you.

Down here on the ground, you are protected by two things. The first is the atmosphere, a blanket of air above you that stops most radiation. Think of it as being under about 33 feet of water, in terms of how much matter sits above your head.

The second shield is even more amazing. Earth itself is a giant magnet. Its magnetic field, called the magnetosphere, bends and traps charged particles, steering most of them away before they ever reach the sky above your house.

Now here is the key to the whole mystery. The space station flies inside that magnetic shield. At 250 miles up, it sits in the inner edge of the protection, far below where the real danger zones begin.

Compare that with the Moon. The Apollo astronauts traveled about 240,000 miles away, leaving the shield behind. The station crew never goes that far. Their whole home stays deep inside the protective bubble, just a short drive in distance from the ground.

But the shield is not perfect, and that is where it gets strange. Above the South Atlantic Ocean, Earth's magnetic field has a weak spot. NASA calls it the South Atlantic Anomaly, and it is one of the biggest radiation hot zones on the station's path.

In that region, the inner Van Allen radiation belt dips lower toward Earth. The station passes through it several times a day, for roughly 10 to 20 minutes at a time. Trapped protons slam into everything, including the walls and the crew.

Inside the station, instruments log it all. Detectors on the walls and tiny dosimeters worn by each astronaut count the radiation passing through. Some computers even glitch when a particle strikes a memory chip while crossing that weak spot.

So how much radiation does a crew member actually get? NASA says astronauts on the station receive an average of about 80 millisieverts over a six month stay. That is roughly 50 to 2,000 millisieverts depending on mission length and solar activity, and we should be careful with that range.

Now compare that with life on Earth. An average American receives about 6.2 millisieverts per year from all sources, according to the National Council on Radiation Protection. So six months on the station can equal about 13 years of ground exposure.

Another comparison. A single chest X-ray gives you about 0.1 millisieverts. A CT scan of the chest, around 7. So a six month stay on the station is something like a dozen CT scans, spread out over half a year.

That sounds like a lot, and honestly, it is. But here is the point. It is not a lethal dose. Sudden radiation sickness starts at around 1,000 millisieverts received in a short time. The station crew stays far below that line.

The real risk is slow. Long term exposure raises the chance of cancer later in life. NASA sets career limits for astronauts, based on keeping the added lifetime cancer risk at or below 3 percent. That is a documented rule, not a guess.

Radiation can also hit the eyes and the brain. Astronauts have reported seeing tiny flashes of light with their eyes closed. Scientists believe these flashes come from cosmic ray particles passing through the eye. Imagine lying in your bunk, and a star blinks inside your head.

Apollo astronauts described the same thing on their way to the Moon, seeing streaks and flashes in the dark. It is one of the few times a person can actually sense radiation. For the rest of it, the body gives you no warning at all.

So what protects the crew inside the walls? Mostly, the walls themselves. The station's modules are built from aluminum and layered shielding, designed first for debris, but they also absorb part of the radiation. Think of it like a thick winter coat, stopping some of the storm.

Some parts of the station are better protected than others. The crew quarters, where each astronaut sleeps, have extra shielding. Water, supplies, and even equipment get placed around the sleeping areas, because hydrogen rich materials like water are good at blocking particles.

That is a simple trick, and a clever one. Plastics like polyethylene work well too, since they contain lots of hydrogen. Engineers have tested these materials on the station, because future deep space ships will need much more protection than this one does.

Now the scary moment. Sometimes the Sun throws a tantrum. A solar particle event can send a wave of high energy protons toward Earth. Ground teams watch the Sun around the clock, with spacecraft like NASA's Solar Dynamics Observatory staring at it.

When a big storm is forecast, mission controllers can warn the crew. The astronauts may move to the best shielded part of the station, and spacewalks can be delayed or canceled. A spacewalk during a storm would be a terrible time to be outside.

The spacesuit offers far less protection than the station. Outside, you are wearing a thin layer of fabric and a helmet. Spacewalks usually last about six or seven hours, so teams plan them carefully, watching the radiation forecast the way a farmer watches the sky.

Here is a piece of good news. The station's orbit helps once more. Because it sits inside the magnetic shield, even during strong storms, the radiation reaching the crew has stayed manageable. Most of the danger from solar storms fades near the equator and grows near the poles.

In fact, the aurora you see in those beautiful photos is the same particle storm, funneled by Earth's magnetic field toward the poles and lighting up the air. The crew floats above it, watching green curtains dance, while the shield does its quiet work.

Of course, NASA does not trust luck. Every astronaut is tracked. Doctors record the dose for each person, each mission, and each year. If an astronaut reaches the career limit, that person is grounded. It is a hard rule, and it has no exceptions for fame.

Scientists also study twin bodies. In NASA's Twins Study, astronaut Scott Kelly spent nearly a year on the station, while his identical twin Mark stayed on Earth. Researchers compared them and found changes in gene activity and in the ends of chromosomes, called telomeres.

Many of those changes returned to normal after he came home, though some did not fully reset within the study period. Results like these are why NASA calls radiation one of the top health risks for long missions, and says there is still a lot to learn.

Now look ahead. Going to Mars changes everything. A trip there would take months each way, far outside Earth's magnetic shield. NASA estimates a round trip could expose a crew to roughly 1,000 millisieverts or more, so protection is a major unsolved challenge.

That is why the Artemis missions matter. The Orion spacecraft carried radiation sensors on its uncrewed Artemis I flight around the Moon in late 2022. Mannequins wearing protective vests rode along, measuring what a real crew would face beyond the shield.

Engineers are testing new ideas too. Thicker water walls, storm shelters, special vests, and even medicines that might protect cells. None of this is magic yet. NASA openly says that a safe, proven answer for a Mars trip is still being worked on.

Meanwhile, back on the station, life goes on. Breakfast, exercise, experiments, a call with family. Your day feels perfectly normal, even as invisible particles pass through the cabin. The crew works, laughs, and sleeps, protected by distance, shielding, and planning.

So why doesn't radiation kill astronauts on the space station? Because Earth's magnetic field covers them, the walls and water absorb part of the rest, doctors track every dose, and teams watch the Sun, ready to warn the crew.

Here is the honest part. Radiation still does add up. The crew accepts a small, measured risk, the way a deep sea diver or a mountain climber does. It is not zero. It is just carefully counted, and kept below strict limits.

Compare it with your own life. A coast to coast flight on an airliner gives you a small extra dose, and frequent flyers collect more. The station is the same story, only turned way up, and watched by far more instruments and doctors.

And now the most surprising detail. The very same invisible storm that worries doctors also gives us the aurora, the glowing curtains that astronauts photograph from the windows. The danger and the beauty are the same thing, seen from two different sides.

scene.testo: So tonight, when you look up, remember the crew floating up there, passing overhead every 90 minutes. Behind every calm sunrise is a shield made of magnetism, metal, water, and people who never stop watching. That is the truth about radiation in orbit.
